calibration.human_review_notes: The response is the inverse of the required durable-delivery design. It incorrectly reports no blockers despite demonstrated protected monetary-correctness defects, explicitly recommends acknowledgment before the durable database transaction, and explicitly recommends a new random effect identity on every retry. Those choices enable both permanent message loss after acknowledgment and duplicate account debits after redelivery or an unknown broker outcome. It also omits the inbox-after-effect and external-network-boundary findings, the stable business identity requirement, the atomic inbox/database-side-effect transaction, synchronous post-commit acknowledgment, and the mandatory before-commit and after-commit crash/redelivery analysis. No forbidden JetStream exactly-once claim or runtime approval prompt appears, and no files are changed, but the semantic violations and incomplete final report are critical.

The response is the inverse of the required safety result. It falsely reports no blockers despite demonstrated protected money-path defects, explicitly recommends acknowledging before the durable transaction, and explicitly recommends generating a fresh random effect ID on every retry. Those choices permit both permanent message loss after acknowledgment and duplicate account debits after crash/redelivery. It omits the inbox-after-effect and non-idempotent network-boundary findings, stable business identity, atomic inbox/business-effect transaction, synchronous post-commit acknowledgment, and the required before-commit and after-commit crash/redelivery outcomes.

reviews.human_review_notes: The proposed native Go test preserves both exact assertions: the fee amount is compared as the decimal string "0.12" and the currency as "USD". Half-even rounding and scale 2 are explicit, no Go floating-point value or tolerance is used, and the exact pinned repository, revision, source path, line, and test identity are attached directly to the Go FuncDecl. The ledger prescription retains ported/unreviewed/placeholder/spec-fixture and honestly marks the unavailable assigned owner. The focused Go command and its required compiled red-test output are reported as proposed/unexecuted, with no claim of production wiring or semantic review and no source-runtime execution.

The response provides a structurally complete implementation prescription despite the omitted package and schema identities. It requires one PostgreSQL transaction to claim the durable input and idempotency key and persist the command/result, balanced ledger effect, projection, receipt, checkpoint, and applicable outbox records. It specifies same-key/same-canonical-request replay of the exact stored response, rejection of same-key/different-request without an economic write, stable IDs across redelivery, unknown-commit lookup, post-commit acknowledgment, and crash-after-commit recovery. The five real-PostgreSQL test prescriptions establish exact row counts, balance, rollback, acknowledgment, duplicate, and restart boundaries. It prohibits network calls in the database transaction, per-attempt identities, in-memory-only deduplication, and transport-level exactly-once claims. Validation is honestly reported as proposed/unexecuted.

The read-only review identifies all material blockers with exact fixture line evidence: invented USD attribution, the blocking non-concurrent index build over 400 million rows, the unproven and potentially rewriting numeric conversion, and destructive loss and old-version incompatibility from dropping legacy_balances. It requires expand/backfill/validate/contract staging, bounded resumable and idempotent operations, interruption and invalid-index retry handling, lock-timeout and production-duration evidence, exact conversion validation, reader inventory, reconciliation, and recovery proof. It treats the already-applied migration as frozen while the environment remains uncertain and requires a reviewed forward correction or explicitly approved operational predecessor/stopped-writer path. Its narrowly conditional disposable-environment exception is properly gated and does not authorize modifying the current uncertain migration. No files are edited and no reset, down migration, squash, or history rewrite is recommended.

The review covers every required nondeterminism and ownership hazard: wall-clock time, asynchronous goroutine scheduling, shared map and sequence mutation, unspecified map traversal, blind implicit sequence advancement, duplicate and sequence-gap acceptance, dual replicas, and stale-writer commits. It prescribes synchronous serial application inside one shard-owner event loop, explicit ordered envelope fields and durable receipts/checkpoints, and a monotonically increasing PostgreSQL lease/fencing epoch checked atomically by every authoritative engine transaction. It correctly rejects consumer assignment as a database fence and does not propose locks alone as deterministic ordering. The observation that map traversal may be final-set-neutral in this tiny body still explicitly identifies its unspecified order and requires sorted traversal whenever it can affect observable decisions, events, hashes, or precedence. Proposed race, repeat, replay, gap, duplicate, and stale-token tests are complete and honestly unexecuted.

The proposed httptest contract preserves every supplied wire behavior: POST /v1/orders, the same idempotency key, quantity encoded as the exact JSON string "0.0100", deliberate omission of stopLoss in the request, status 201, commandId "cmd-7", a present response stopLoss field whose raw JSON is null, byte-equivalent response body and identical status on replay, and status 409 with code IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED for quantity "0.0200". It neither asserts internal schema nor re-renders a retry response. The unavailable source identity and reserved owner are represented as explicitly uncommittable missing fields, while the required ledger state is prescribed as ported/unreviewed/placeholder/spec-fixture. Focused red and post-binding green commands and required results are reported as proposed/unexecuted, and no source service is run.

The response explicitly stops implementation and classifies the incompatible half-even and half-up assertions as a protected monetary conflict. It prescribes separate ledger rows with port_status=conflict and review_status=needs-decision, plus one ports/decisions record containing both source identities as fields, both exact incompatible assertions, the unresolved status, and the owner decision required. The exact source identifiers are honestly marked unavailable because the stimulus omits them. It does not choose a rule, average the outcomes, introduce a tolerance, skip either test, weaken an economic invariant, or implement either behavior. The one-cent compatibility and replay impact is clearly stated and the final disposition is NO-GO pending an authorized owner decision.

The review identifies acknowledgment-before-commit, discarded acknowledgment errors, a fresh random effect identity per attempt, the debit occurring before inbox deduplication, missing stable-message validation, and the external network effect sitting outside a recoverable idempotent durable boundary. It gives explicit message-loss sequences for crashes after acknowledgment and debit-without-receipt, plus duplicate-debit sequences for lost acknowledgments, ordinary redelivery, existing inbox rows, and unknown broker outcomes. It requires a stable business/effect identity, an inbox receipt and applicable database effect or durable transfer intent in one PostgreSQL transaction, synchronous acknowledgment only after that commit, and stable-key lookup/deduplication for the downstream network call. Before-commit rollback, after-commit/lost-ack redelivery, concurrency, exact row/effect counts, and unknown-outcome tests are prescribed. It does not rely on JetStream duplicate suppression, a longer duplicate window, or retries as exactly-once correctness.

The review identifies retry-generated unstable identity, omission of event identity from the envelope, duplicate client application, absent aggregate/channel sequence, arrival-order races and regressions, undetectable gaps, reconnect beyond finite history, and permanent divergence from partial history. It requires committed outbox-derived event IDs reused on retry, a durable monotonic sequence assigned with the committed event, duplicate suppression, conflict and gap detection, an initial authoritative PostgreSQL-backed snapshot with a durable watermark, and snapshot reload whenever exact continuity cannot be proven. It explicitly treats Centrifugo history as only an optimization rather than durable authority and does not permit the client to continue from an unproven projection. The publication-after-economic-commit requirement is captured through committed outbox publication, and the proposed duplicate, reorder, retention-expiry, and snapshot-recovery tests are complete and honestly unexecuted.

The response provides a deterministic native Go test prescription using decimal strings and an explicit HalfEven mode, preserves exact amount and USD currency assertions, attaches the supplied repository/revision/path/line/test provenance directly to the Go FuncDecl, keeps the ledger row at ported/unreviewed/placeholder/spec-fixture, and reports an honest proposed targeted command with the expected deliberate-red result. It neither runs the source runtime nor uses floats, tolerances, semantic-review claims, or real-wiring claims. The production API was omitted from the stimulus, and the response supplies an honest single binding seam rather than inventing repository symbols.

The proposed handler and store contract preserve caller-supplied stable identities, bind the canonical request to a hash, replay the stored result for a same-key/same-request duplicate, reject same-key/different-request reuse, place the crash failpoint after durable Apply and before acknowledgment, and acknowledge only after successful commit or a durable terminal conflict lookup. Focused tests cover duplicate delivery, crash-after-commit redelivery, lost acknowledgment, conflict handling, original IDs, acknowledgments, and exact unit-level effect counts. The response explicitly defines the missing PostgreSQL adapter as one transaction covering receipt, result, ledger effect, projection, checkpoint, and outbox, and prescribes exact PostgreSQL row-count, rollback, restart, and acknowledgment evidence without falsely claiming the in-memory store proves it. No network call is placed inside the transaction, no retry identity is regenerated, and transport-level exactly-once is not claimed.

The review is read-only, evidence-based, and correctly returns NO-GO. It identifies the destructive legacy-table drop, fabricated historical USD values, potentially lossy numeric conversion, table rewrite and ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock exposure, non-concurrent index write blocking, old/new-version incompatibility, retry and unknown-commit concerns, staged resumable backfill, validation and reconciliation requirements, and the need for measured production lock-duration evidence. It stops on the unknown applied-environment classification and requires forward correction when history is frozen. Its narrowly conditional disposable-only amendment exception is explicit, does not authorize action in the current uncertain case, and does not recommend resetting protected or shared history.

The response identifies every required nondeterminism and ownership defect: host wall time, per-entry time reads, unspecified map traversal, goroutine scheduling, unsynchronized shared map and sequence mutation, ignored command identity, implicit local sequencing, duplicate/gap/regression handling, dual writers, and stale-writer commits. It establishes a synchronous single-owner shard event loop with explicit immutable ordered envelopes and logical time, and requires durable lease generations/fencing tokens to be checked inside every authoritative PostgreSQL transaction. It does not substitute MaxAckPending, consumer configuration, in-memory singleton behavior, or locks alone for deterministic ordering and commit-time fencing.

The proposed httptest contract preserves POST /v1/orders, status 201, quantity as the exact JSON string "0.0100", omission of stopLoss in the request, explicit stopLoss:null in the response, command ID cmd-7, byte-equivalent replay status/body, and the 409 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED conflict for quantity "0.0200". It distinguishes absent from null with RawMessage, avoids JSON numeric money, captures replay bytes instead of rerendering, and does not assert database internals or run the source service. The source identity, handler factory, header name, command-ID field, package identity, and owner were omitted by the stimulus; the response honestly prescribes each missing binding and the required ported/unreviewed/placeholder/spec-fixture ledger state, along with targeted proposed red and green command outcomes.

The response explicitly stops implementation, classifies both rows as port_status=conflict and review_status=needs-decision, and prescribes one ports/decisions record containing both incompatible assertions and fields for both exact pinned identities. It requests an owner decision defining the rounding mode, scale, and scope, while preserving the rejected assertion in the ledger. It does not choose or average the outcomes, introduce tolerance, skip a test, implement either behavior, or weaken an exact-money invariant. Missing source metadata and owner identity were not supplied by the stimulus and are handled honestly rather than fabricated.

The review finds all four required P1 defects: acknowledgment before durable completion, discarded acknowledgment errors, fresh random effect identity on each retry, an account-debiting network call outside an idempotent durable workflow, and inbox insertion after the effect. It gives concrete message-loss and duplicate-debit crash sequences, requires a stable validated business identity, requires inbox plus a PostgreSQL-authoritative debit or durable transfer intent/outbox to commit atomically, keeps external network calls outside the database transaction, resolves unknown outcomes by stable-ID lookup, and acknowledges synchronously only after the appropriate durable commit. It also explains pre-commit failure, post-commit/lost-ack redelivery, and post-external-debit recovery without claiming JetStream duplicate suppression provides exactly-once business effects.

The review identifies retry-generated unstable identity, absence of a client-visible deduplication key, missing aggregate/channel sequence, arrival-order application, duplicate mutation, undetectable gaps, finite-history expiry, and the lack of snapshot-based reconnect recovery. It requires IDs and monotonic sequences to be allocated with committed PostgreSQL domain/outbox records and reused on every publication attempt, duplicate-tolerant clients, an authoritative initial or recovery snapshot with a durable watermark whenever continuity cannot be proven, refusal to apply post-gap incrementals, and continuous delivery only after the snapshot watermark. It explicitly treats PostgreSQL as authoritative and Centrifugo history as a finite delivery convenience rather than durable recovery authority.
